newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-City of Gold challenges S.Africa sex laws.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-City of Gold challenges S.Africa sex laws.

text.p: Top prize for hip South Africans is a pair of Doc Martens boots, retailing at $120. For sex workers in the City of Gold, that means turning two tricks.
Despite the stigma of prostitution, sex is selling fast in South Africa and teenage runaways as young as 14 are quickly initiated into brothels or massage parlours.
In the newly politically correct South Africa they are called sex workers rather than prostitutes or whores, but their lives remain seedy litanies of drugs and abuse.

White-ruled South Africa, which for a long time banned sex between the races, was among the world's most conservative states when it came to fighting social problems such as unwanted pregnancies, drug abuse, prostitution and pornography.

Black-led South Africa, still a very religious country and by no means on a course towards permissiveness, has eased stringent film and book censorship and is liberalising the law to afford women easy access to legal abortions.

Determined to end discrimination against women, policy-makers in South Africa's wealthiest region, Gauteng, now hope to correct a criminal system that penalises the prostitutes but not the men who buy their services.
Prostitutes usually pay fines ranging from $30 to more than $200. Proposed penalties for clients have not been decided.

A prostitute in rehabilitation, identified only as Maxine, has urged lawmakers to overturn what she said was the current law's indifference to the multiple rape and abuse often meted out to women and girls by clients and pimps.
"I'm worried about the girls still suffering out there in a living hell," Maxine, now off the beat and five months pregnant, told a public hearing called to debate policy.
"We are the vulnerable people with no one to turn to. Whatever new law is set, it must recognise this."

Maxine spoke of gang rapes she had to endure, and the multiple personality disorder she developed to cope with the sordid underworld of prostitution. Currently in intensive psychological therapy, she said:
"That is my future: trying to recover from the years of damage and abuse."

Another ex-prostitute, Sophie, said she had resorted to prostitution at the age of 14 when, as a runaway from home, her minimal school education ruled out other jobs. Saying her way out of prostitution was a hard-won battle rather than a sudden revelation, she urged:
"There are women out there who need help, not a lesson in morality. They need alternatives."
A post-apartheid policy on the sex industry in Gauteng, centred on Johannesburg, will go to the provincial cabinet in February.
It is expected to drop the criminal penalties against prostitutes but propose heavy penalties for pimps who lure children into the industry.
"We're going for the middle ground: decriminalisation with controls," said a policing ministry official, Sylvester Rakgoadi.

"Our position is informed by the rights the new constitution gives to our citizens -- free economic activity, health care services and recourse to the law," he told Reuters. "Prostitutes should have these rights like any other person."

The House, a shelter set up six years ago to rehabilitate child prostitutes in Johannesburg's rough inner-city Hillbrow area, says there are 10,000 children working in the sex industry nationwide with little or no state or community help.

"The general feeling towards them is still not empathy or sympathy but, like the abortion issue, is reserved to remain a moot point in the hearts of even the greatest philanthropists," said The House's Jean du Plessis.
"Men and women are culturally conditioned to place all the blame for prostitution on women. It's like saying black people were powerless in the previous regime because they liked it."
Rakgoadi said opening up state health and care facilities for sex workers would be "a challenge" as many employees rejected prostitution as immoral.
"It will mean changing mind-sets in the government services," he acknowledged.

In Johannesburg alone, 8,000 women sell sex in the squalid inner city, wealthy suburbs and informal township pubs. The city's commercial sex trade generates an estimated $8.6 million a month, most of which is spent on accommodation and drugs.
Nationally there are 50,000 prostitutes amidst a population of about nine million males over the age of 18. Clients are on average middle-class men, over 35 and married.
